match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how a measurement error carries through a calculation into an area or volume; the closest cards cover absolute error and limits of accuracy, percentage error, or random and systematic error, and the scaling card is about similar shapes rather than measurement error.

draft.title: How measurement errors affect results
card: A measured length can be a little different from the actual length. This is a measurement error.
When the length is used in a calculation, the error grows. Area of a square = side × side, so the error is carried into both sides.
Example: a square has an actual side of 21 cm, but it is measured as 20 cm. The side is out by 1 cm. The area is 441 cm² actual and 400 cm² measured, so it is out by 41 cm².
Volume of a cube = edge × edge × edge, so a small error in the edge grows even more.
draft.remember: A small error in a length becomes a larger error in area or volume.

a.q: A square's side is measured as 20 cm, but it is actually 21 cm. By how much is the area out?
a.why: The actual area is 21² = 441 cm² and the measured area is 20² = 400 cm². The difference is 41 cm². The side error of 1 cm does not stay at 1: it grows when the side is squared.

b.q: A cube's edge is measured as 10 cm, but it is actually 11 cm. By how much is the volume out?
b.why: The actual volume is 11³ = 1331 cm³ and the measured volume is 10³ = 1000 cm³. The difference is 331 cm³. A 1 cm error in the edge becomes a much larger error in volume.
b.clue: Cube both edge lengths, then find the difference.

problems.detail: Question a uses exactly the same numbers as the card's worked example (20 cm measured, 21 cm actual, out by 41 cm²). A student can copy the answer from the card without doing or understanding the calculation. Use different side lengths.

final.title: How measurement errors affect results
card: A measured length can be a little different from the actual length. This is a measurement error.
When the length is used in a calculation, the error grows. Area of a square \(=\) side \(\times\) side, so the error is carried into both sides.

Example: a square has an actual side of 21 cm, but it is measured as 20 cm. The side is out by 1 cm. The area is \(441 \text{ cm}^{2}\) actual and \(400 \text{ cm}^{2}\) measured, so it is out by \(41 \text{ cm}^{2}\).
Volume of a cube \(=\) edge \(\times\) edge \(\times\) edge, so a small error in the edge grows even more. Work out both results, then subtract.

a.why: The actual area is \(13^{2} = 169 \text{ cm}^{2}\) and the measured area is \(12^{2} = 144 \text{ cm}^{2}\). The difference is \(25 \text{ cm}^{2}\). The side error of 1 cm does not stay at 1: it grows when the side is squared.

b.q: A cube's edge is measured as 10 cm, but it is actually 11 cm. By how much is the volume out?
b.why: The actual volume is \(11^{3} = 1331 \text{ cm}^{3}\) and the measured volume is \(10^{3} = 1000 \text{ cm}^{3}\). The difference is \(331 \text{ cm}^{3}\). A 1 cm error in the edge becomes a much larger error in volume.
b.clue: Cube both edge lengths, then find the difference.
